title: Mistretta v. United States
lead: A defendant sentenced under the new federal Guidelines challenges both the policy discretion Congress delegated and the structure of a commission placed within the Judicial Branch.

actors.name: Mistretta
actors.role: Defendant convicted of conspiracy to distribute cocaine who challenged the federal sentencing system.

actors.name: United States Sentencing Commission
actors.role: Independent statutory body within the Judicial Branch that promulgated binding sentencing guidelines under the system reviewed.

actors.name: Congress and the President
actors.role: Congress established the Commission and its boundaries; the President appointed members with Senate consent and held limited removal authority.

proceedings: The Western District of Missouri rejected the constitutional challenge and imposed a guideline sentence.
Mistretta appealed to the Eighth Circuit; both sides sought Supreme Court review before appellate judgment.
The Supreme Court affirmed the district court on January 18, 1989, by eight votes to one.
limits: The account describes the binding-guidelines system reviewed in 1989, not later sentencing law. The Court reserved compulsory service by an individual judge, equivalent delegation to an actual court, and specified capital-punishment and salary questions.

review.basis: Fresh comparison with the complete effective canonical brief; no new independent opinion verification claimed.

sections.title: Congress replaces a discretionary sentencing arrangement with a commission system
sections.cue: What problems and institutional design preceded Mistretta’s prosecution?
paragraphs: Before the Sentencing Reform Act of 1984, Congress supplied broad sentencing ranges, district judges chose sentences with great appellate deference, and executive parole officials often determined actual imprisonment. Congress became dissatisfied with disparities among similar offenders, uncertain time served, and the limits of rehabilitation and parole as corrections. Sentencing institutes and Parole Commission guidelines had not eliminated those problems.

The Act created basically determinate sentences with good-behavior reductions and prospectively abolished parole under its then-prescribed schedule. Congress rejected fixed sentences and purely advisory guidance. The new Guidelines bound courts, permitting departure for aggravating or mitigating circumstances the Commission had not adequately considered. Judges explained sentences and gave specific departure reasons. Defendants could appeal above-range sentences, the government below-range sentences, and either side incorrect application.

Congress placed an independent United States Sentencing Commission within the Judicial Branch. Seven voting members were presidentially appointed with Senate confirmation; at least three were federal judges selected after consideration of six Judicial Conference nominees. No more than four belonged to one political party. The Attorney General or a designee and, temporarily, the Parole Commission chair participated without votes. Voting members ordinarily served six-year terms, limited to two full terms, and could be removed by the President only for neglect, malfeasance, or other good cause.

The Commission formulated and revised guidelines, consulted criminal-justice officials, reported amendments and annual analyses, recommended statutory penalty changes, issued policy statements, collected records from over 40,000 sentences yearly, and conducted training and administration.

sources.pinpoint: 488 U.S. at 363–370 & n.4; Sentencing system and statutory design

sections.title: A cocaine indictment produces a constitutional challenge and direct Supreme Court review
sections.cue: What sentence and arguments were actually before the Court?
paragraphs: On December 10, 1987, Mistretta and another defendant were indicted on three counts arising from a cocaine sale. Mistretta challenged the Guidelines as an excessive delegation and the Commission as inconsistent with separation of powers. The Western District of Missouri rejected the challenge, calling the Commission executive despite its statutory placement and comparing the Guidelines to substantive agency rules. The Supreme Court later supplied its own structural analysis rather than simply adopting that characterization.

Mistretta pleaded guilty to conspiracy to distribute cocaine under 21 U.S.C. §§ 846 and 841(b)(1)(B). On the government’s motion, the other counts were dismissed. The court imposed eighteen months’ imprisonment, three years of supervised release, a $1,000 fine, and a $50 special assessment. Mistretta appealed to the Eighth Circuit, but both sides sought Supreme Court review before judgment. The Court accepted because of imperative public importance and lower-court disagreement.

Mistretta challenged discretion to rank crimes and weigh offender characteristics. He also argued that judicial placement mixed legislative and judicial power; judge-membership threatened independence and impartiality; policymaking with nonjudges shared judicial power improperly; and presidential appointment and removal introduced political influence over judges.

sections.title: Eight Justices find detailed guidance for a difficult delegated task
sections.cue: Which statutory limits supplied an intelligible principle?
paragraphs: Justice Blackmun wrote for Chief Justice Rehnquist and Justices Brennan, White, Marshall, Stevens, O’Connor, and Kennedy. Congress could obtain assistance by stating policy, identifying the implementing institution, and fixing boundaries that permitted review for fidelity to legislative will. Substantial judgment and subsidiary policy choices did not themselves violate nondelegation.

The Act specified certainty, fairness, reduced unwarranted disparity with appropriate flexibility, and improved knowledge of human behavior. It identified punishment’s purposes and rejected imprisonment to promote rehabilitation. Guidelines had to remain within statutory penalties; imprisonment ranges ordinarily could spread no more than twenty-five percent or six months, whichever was greater, with a life maximum allowed when the minimum was thirty years.

Congress supplied seven offense considerations and eleven offender characteristics, directed treatment of specified recidivists and serious offenses, and identified circumstances favoring imprisonment, alternatives, or mitigation. Race, sex, national origin, creed, and socioeconomic status were prohibited, and possible proxies restricted. Existing averages supplied a starting point, not a command to preserve inadequate punishments. These instructions produced a hierarchy from near-maximum imprisonment to alternatives, leaving important but bounded discretion for an intricate task.

Footnote 11 assumed without deciding authority to implement existing statutory death penalties consistently with Supreme Court precedent while denying power to create a new capital offense. Brennan did not join that footnote. Neither the footnote nor the judgment finally adjudicated the disputed capital-punishment authority.

sources.pinpoint: 488 U.S. at 371–379 & nn.8–11; Nondelegation holding and statutory constraints

sections.title: Judicial placement does not make the Commission a court
sections.cue: Why did the majority permit this combination of functions?
paragraphs: The majority rejected airtight separation as the constitutional test. It asked whether the structure accumulated power improperly, encroached on assigned functions, or damaged judicial integrity. Procedural rulemaking, judicial councils, and administrative institutions showed that the Judicial Branch could perform some nonadjudicatory work. Sentencing had always involved all three branches, and judges had long made judgments of the type centralized in the Guidelines.

The Court acknowledged that sentencing policy was more political and substantive than ordinary procedural rules. It did not label the Guidelines merely procedural to avoid that difficulty. Instead it examined practical consequences. The Commission was not a court, exercised no judicial power, and was neither controlled by nor accountable to the Judiciary. Judges could form a minority. Congress could revise or revoke the Guidelines, the President had limited removal power, and notice and comment applied. Equivalent authority delegated to an actual court was expressly reserved.

The Guidelines created no new crimes and did not replace statutory minimum or maximum penalties; they constrained discretion judges formerly exercised. Placement within the Judicial Branch neither accumulated new judicial power at others’ expense nor prevented adjudication. The Executive had not previously exercised the particular authority assigned and retained appointment, removal, and nonvoting participation relationships despite the Commission’s location.

sources.pinpoint: 488 U.S. at 380–397 & nn.12–20; Judicial placement and separation of powers

sections.title: The majority separates service as commissioner from service as a judge
sections.cue: Why did presidential removal from the Commission not control adjudication?
paragraphs: Judges serving on the Commission exercised administrative authority under separate appointments, not Article III jurisdiction. Unlike legislators, they were not subject to a constitutional incompatibility clause. Historical extrajudicial service and decisions including Hayburn’s Case and Ferreira supported a distinction between court judgments and judges acting as individual commissioners, though the history did not bless every assignment.

No particular judge could be compelled to accept service under the Court’s construction, and compulsory individual service remained unresolved. Participation in writing rules did not automatically require recusal from every case applying them. Here judicial expertise informed sentencing without employing judicial prestige to define crimes or enforce prosecutions. Sharing Commission work with nonjudges therefore did not distribute Article III power.

Removal from the Commission could not remove a judge from the bench, reduce Article III status, or diminish judicial salary. Good-cause limits supplied additional independence. The Court reserved treatment of a district judge’s additional commissioner salary. The issue was presidential influence over judging, not whether Congress restricted removal of executive officials too much. Removing a judge from this nonadjudicatory position did not give the President control over adjudication.

sources.pinpoint: 488 U.S. at 397–412 & nn.21–35; Judicial membership and presidential control

sections.title: Scalia accepts the statutory guidance but rejects freestanding lawmaking
sections.cue: Where did the lone dissent locate the constitutional defect?
paragraphs: Justice Scalia, dissenting alone, agreed that the Act’s standards met the Court’s delegation precedents. Every law leaves judgment to its administrators or interpreters, and determining when discretion becomes excessive entails difficult questions of degree for which Congress may be better equipped.

His objection concerned the recipient and nature of the power. Rulemaking ordinarily accompanied lawful executive administration or judicial adjudication. Even an agency devoted to rulemaking could fit if controlled by the President and ancillary to executive authority. This Commission, however, adjudicated no cases, exercised no executive function, and was controlled by neither courts nor the President. Data collection and advice did not supply the missing function.

Scalia considered its binding sentencing policy freestanding lawmaking, which a judicial label could not cure. Politically insulated expert legislatures might appear attractive while avoiding the cost of strengthening an existing branch. Judging acceptable interbranch mixing case by case could not replace the prescribed constitutional structure. He would reverse; usefulness did not save an additional legislative institution. His own capital-punishment footnote likewise discussed a disputed possible authority, not an actual exercise approved by the Court.

On January 18, 1989, the Court affirmed the district court in both cases before it. The two assigned excerpts emphasize different aspects of this same judgment, not separate litigation stages. The holding sustained this Act against the presented delegation and separation-of-powers challenges without approving every judicial commission or later change in sentencing law.

sources.pinpoint: 488 U.S. at 412–427 & Scalia nn.1–3; Exact judgment and limits; Decision and assigned setting
